identity.title: Resting heart rate >100/min (and postural pulse increment)

technique.how: Count the radial or apical pulse for a full 60 seconds with the patient resting supine for at least 2 minutes; confirm rhythm on the monitor or ECG. For the postural increment, re-count after 1 minute of standing (not sitting) and record the change in beats/min, noting any dizziness severe enough to prevent standing.
technique.prerequisites: Patient at rest, afebrile-state noted, no pain or anxiety stimulus at the time of counting; monitor rhythm strip available if irregular.
technique.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is hypotensive, syncopal or at fall risk to obtain postural vitals.

interpretation.positive_finding: Resting tachycardia is non-specific but sensitive for several emergencies: in tamponade it is present in about 77% of cases. A postural pulse rise >=30/min or inability to stand from dizziness is highly specific (98%) for large acute blood loss and present in 97% after 630-1150 mL phlebotomy.
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal resting heart rate does not exclude blood loss, PE or tamponade; supine tachycardia is frequently absent after up to 1150 mL blood loss, and a postural pulse increment misses most moderate (450-630 mL) losses (sensitivity 22%).
interpretation.pitfalls: Beta-blockers, pacemakers, athletes and conduction disease blunt tachycardia; fever, pain, anxiety, anaemia and hyperthyroidism cause it without hypovolaemia. The postural increment requires standing for a minute; sitting vitals are insensitive.
interpretation.changes_what: Unexplained resting HR >100: search for bleeding, sepsis, PE, tamponade, thyrotoxicosis; postural rise >=30 or severe postural dizziness: treat as large-volume loss and resuscitate.

estimates.target_condition: COMPOSITE: postural pulse increment >=30 beats/min OR severe postural dizziness (unable to stand for vitals), for LARGE acute blood loss (630-1150 mL phlebotomy)
estimates.population: Healthy volunteers undergoing phlebotomy of up to 1150 mL in pooled studies (RCE review of 10 volunteer studies, MEDLINE 1966-1997)
estimates.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (large = 630-1150 mL)
estimates.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)

estimates.target_condition: COMPOSITE: postural pulse increment >=30 beats/min OR severe postural dizziness, for MODERATE acute blood loss (450-630 mL phlebotomy)
estimates.population: Healthy volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled volunteer studies in RCE review)
estimates.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (moderate = 450-630 mL)
estimates.quote: The presence of either finding has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
estimates.location: Abstract, Results (specificity 98% from the same sentence: 'the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)')

estimates.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade (echocardiographic/clinical tamponade among patients with pericardial effusion); finding = tachycardia (resting heart rate above normal, threshold not specified in abstract)
estimates.population: Patients with known tamponade or referred for pericardiocentesis with known effusion, 8 studies (RCE systematic review, MEDLINE 1966-2006)
estimates.reference_standard: Tamponade diagnosed by echocardiography and/or hemodynamic response to pericardiocentesis

sources.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
Roy CL, Minor MA, Brookhart MA, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with a pericardial effusion have cardiac tamponade? JAMA. 2007;297(16):1810-1818.
Chunilal SD, Eikelboom JW, Attia J, Miniati M, Panju AA, Simel DL, Ginsberg JS. Does this patient have pulmonary embolism? JAMA. 2003;290(21):2849-2858.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal heart rate to exclude haemorrhage, PE or tamponade, especially in beta-blocked or elderly patients; do not perform standing vitals in a patient who is hypotensive or has already had syncope.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Resting HR >100 with hypotension, rising lactate, new confusion or a pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg is shock until proven otherwise; escalate and resuscitate rather than observe.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Pulse counting is reliable when done for 60 s; postural measurements are technique-sensitive (standing, not sitting; wait 1 minute). No kappa reported in the RCE abstracts.

extraction_notes: All three PMIDs confirmed; JAMA full texts not in PMC, so estimates come from abstracts ('Abstract, Results'). The hypovolaemia RCE gives only a COMPOSITE (postural pulse increment >=30/min OR severe postural dizziness), entered with the COMPOSITE prefix; the sensitivity of supine tachycardia alone for blood loss is described as 'frequently absent' but the number is not in the abstract (only supine hypotension sensitivity 33% is), so it is not entered. Volunteer phlebotomy is not a clinical cohort, hence no prevalence. Tamponade RCE (PMID 17456823) reports pooled sensitivity of tachycardia only (case-series-type studies), no specificity or LR; threshold for tachycardia not given in abstract. PE RCE (PMID 14657070) evaluates gestalt and prediction rules only and provides no tachycardia-specific accuracy; cited as context only. No estimate has this single sign's own sens/spec or LR pair, so status is partially_quantified.
